query: How do I set up Chart.js v4.5.1 in a new project using npm with tree-shaking instead of `chart.js/auto`, register only the components I need for a line chart, configure global defaults for responsive behavior, and then write a helper function that updates the chart's dataset dynamically and properly destroys the old instance before re-rendering so we don't get memory leaks?

We have a high-throughput genomics data pipeline running on Spring Boot 3.2 that ingests VCF files from sequencing instruments via a REST API, processes variant calls through a chain of analysis steps, and stores results in PostgreSQL. Right now the blocking I/O on the database and file parsing is killing our throughput — we're maxing out at ~200 concurrent sample submissions before the thread pool is exhausted. I want to refactor the request handling layer to use virtual threads (Project Loom) with the new `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`, but I also need to integrate structured concurrency via `StructuredTaskScope` so that when we fan out a single sample submission into parallel tasks (annotation lookup, quality scoring, and dbSNP cross-reference), if any subtask fails we cancel the siblings cleanly. Additionally, our variant model hierarchy (`Variant`, `SNP extends Variant`, `Indel extends Variant`, `StructuralVariant extends Variant`) would benefit from using sealed classes and switch expressions with pattern matching to replace the current visitor-pattern dispatch in the filtering engine. Can you rewrite the `VariantIngestionController`, the `AnalysisFanOutService`, and the `VariantFilter` classes with all of these modern Java 21 features, making sure the virtual thread integration plays nicely with Spring Boot's auto-configuration and that the `StructuredTaskScope` properly handles the scoped values we use for tenant context propagation?

Our ML platform team needs to decide how to handle model serving for a new real-time fraud detection system. We have three architecture options: (1) deploy models directly into our Go transaction-processing microservice using ONNX Runtime, which is fast but couples model updates to service deploys; (2) stand up a separate Python-based model server (Triton or TorchServe) behind gRPC, which decouples things but adds ~15ms latency and another failure point; (3) use a sidecar pattern with a Rust inference engine per pod, which is novel but our team has zero Rust experience. We're under pressure because the last project chose option 2 and had a major outage during Black Friday — but I don't want us to overreact to that one bad outcome and throw out an architecturally sound approach just because it failed once under extreme load. Can you help me think through this as a set of explicit bets? For each option, lay out the key uncertainties (latency p99, deployment complexity, team ramp-up time, failure blast radius), assign rough probability ranges to the risk scenarios, and evaluate which option has the best expected value given our constraints — separating the quality of each architectural decision from the outcome of that one Black Friday incident? Also, for whichever option you recommend, sketch out the core service integration code (Go client calling the inference layer) so I can prototype it this week.

We're scaling our outbound sales motion and I want to build a systematic cold email testing framework in Python at `~/repos/outreach-engine/`. Here's what I need: create a module that manages multi-variant cold email campaigns where we can define subject lines, opening hooks, CTAs, and email body templates as independent variables, then assign prospects to test cells using proper randomization with configurable traffic splits (e.g., 80/20 holdout or even splits across variants). It should track opens, replies, and positive replies per variant, calculate statistical significance using a two-proportion z-test so we know when we have a real winner vs. noise, and flag when we've hit minimum sample sizes for each cell. I also want a `results_dashboard.py` script that outputs a summary table showing each variant's conversion rate, confidence intervals, lift over control, and p-values — plus recommendations on whether to keep testing or declare a winner and roll out. Make sure the system supports sequential testing so we're not just peeking at results and fooling ourselves with false positives. We've been burned before by calling winners too early on 50-email samples and then seeing performance revert.

We're preparing for a major compliance audit on our healthcare data platform and need to tackle three parallel workstreams simultaneously: (1) spin up a specialized agent with access to our PostgreSQL database via MCP to scan all 120+ tables for columns containing PHI/PII that aren't properly encrypted at rest, generating a full inventory report; (2) have another agent with filesystem and GitHub MCP access audit our entire `patient-services` monorepo (about 300K lines of Java/Spring Boot) for HIPAA violations — hardcoded credentials, unmasked log outputs, missing audit trails on data access endpoints, and any API routes that return patient data without requiring the `X-Consent-Token` header; and (3) a third agent that connects to our AWS MCP tools to verify that all S3 buckets containing medical records have versioning enabled, access logging turned on, and bucket policies that deny non-SSL requests. Each workstream will take a while and I want to be able to check in on their progress independently. Once all three finish, compile their findings into a single prioritized remediation plan ranked by HIPAA risk severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low) with estimated engineering effort for each item, formatted as a markdown document I can present to our CISO on Thursday.

We're migrating our "HealthBridge" telemedicine platform from a monolithic architecture to microservices running on Kubernetes across three regional clusters (us-east, eu-west, ap-south). I need help designing the complete Istio service mesh configuration for this. Specifically: (1) Set up multi-cluster mesh federation across all three regions with shared trust domain and intermediate CAs per cluster, including the meshconfig, remote secrets, and east-west gateway definitions. (2) Configure fine-grained traffic management — we need canary deployments for our `consultation-service` with header-based routing so internal QA gets v2 while production users stay on v1, plus locality-aware load balancing that keeps APAC patient video streams in ap-south but fails over to us-east if ap-south drops below 2 healthy endpoints. (3) Define AuthorizationPolicies and PeerAuthentication resources that enforce strict mTLS mesh-wide but allow our legacy `billing-gateway` (non-mesh VM workload registered via WorkloadEntry) to communicate with `payment-service` using PERMISSIVE mode, and restrict the `patient-records` service so only `consultation-service` and `prescription-service` ServiceAccounts can reach it on specific paths. (4) Integrate the mesh telemetry with our existing Prometheus/Grafana/Jaeger stack — I want to configure EnvoyFilter resources to add custom metrics tracking per-tenant request latency (tenant ID is in a JWT claim), set up distributed tracing propagation across the three clusters, and create Kiali dashboards that show cross-cluster traffic flows. Please provide the full YAML manifests, explain any gotchas with Istio's DNS proxying in multi-cluster, and flag if there are known issues with the east-west gateway when running Istio 1.20+ with the ambient mesh data plane.

Our C# solution "FinLedger" has about 45 projects spanning domain models, API controllers, and background workers — we recently added several new cross-project dependencies and I need you to rebuild the code graph index for the entire repository using ragsharp-graph so we can query class-level dependencies with accurate line numbers, then use that updated graph to find every transitive dependency chain from `FinLedger.Api` down to `FinLedger.Core.Entities` and flag any circular references.

Build me a Python tool that takes a single vertical video file as input and automatically generates platform-optimized export packages for TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts, and Facebook Reels. For each platform it should: detect the ideal trim points to hit that platform's sweet-spot duration, auto-generate three hook variants for the first 1-3 seconds using text overlay (burned-in captions with different attention-grabbing opening lines), analyze the audio track to find a natural loop point so the video seamlessly replays, add a subtle zoom or motion effect in the first 0.5s to stop the scroll, and output a metadata JSON per platform containing the recommended posting time window (weekday + hour range in UTC), a set of 5 hashtags sized for that platform's discovery algorithm, a caption draft under the character limit with a CTA, and a flag for whether the current aspect ratio needs letterbox padding or cropping. I also want a `--trending` flag that hits TikTok's Creative Center API (or scrapes if no API) to pull this week's trending sounds and suggests the top 3 that match the video's vibe based on BPM and energy. The whole thing should be pip-installable with a CLI entry point.

Our open-source project `screenplay-toolkit` on GitHub (github.com/narrativedev/screenplay-toolkit) is a Python library that analyzes screenplay `.fountain` files for structural and character development issues — think of it as a linter for screenwriters. We've gotten a flood of new issues and PRs over the past month and I need help on two fronts simultaneously. First, can you triage the open issues, review pending PRs, check for stale branches, and give me a maintenance report including contributor activity and anything that needs my immediate attention? Second, several of the recent issues (specifically #142, #158, and #171) are all reporting that our character arc validation module is producing false positives — it's flagging Michael Corleone-style negative arcs as "broken arcs" and treating flat/steadfast arcs (like the James Bond archetype) as "missing transformation." It also seems to completely miss the distinction between a transformational arc like Tootsie's Michael Dorsey and a disillusionment arc like Jim in Empire of the Sun. I need you to review the logic in `arc_checker.py`, propose fixes that correctly validate positive, negative, transformational, and flat arc types with proper test cases referencing classic film examples, and then draft PR descriptions for the fixes so I can get community feedback before merging. Also flag if any of the open PRs from contributors are already attempting to address this so we don't duplicate work.

Our security team just published an internal workshop recording at https://securityteam.internal/recordings/pam-migration-2024.mp4 where they walk through our entire migration plan from CyberArk to senhasegura, including the new credential vaulting policies, A2A module configurations for our Jenkins and Kubernetes pipelines, DSM CLI setup for developer workstations, and the External Secrets Operator integration with our EKS clusters. I missed the live session and the slides aren't available yet. Can you pull out a detailed summary of the recording — specifically the step-by-step migration timeline, which credential types they're moving first, the senhasegura DSM CLI commands they recommend for local dev secret injection, the MySafe personal credential policies they're rolling out, and how they plan to wire up the SSH key rotation schedule? Also, based on what they outlined, draft me a working senhasegura A2A authorization config and an ExternalSecret manifest that would match what they described for our `payments-service` namespace.

Set up a new Deepnote project for our InsightPulseAI data lab that will serve as the central workspace for our retail analytics team. We need notebooks organized into three areas: (1) exploratory analysis of customer purchase patterns, (2) scheduled ETL jobs that pull from our Snowflake warehouse and produce Superset-ready summary tables for the BI team, and (3) a sandbox area for ad-hoc queries. For the project scaffold, generate a shared setup configuration that includes pre-commit security hooks to prevent accidental credential leaks in notebook outputs, a standard Claude-compatible framework structure template so our AI-assisted workflows integrate cleanly, and auto-detection of which Python framework each notebook is using (pandas vs. PySpark vs. Polars) so the right linting and dependency configs get applied automatically. The detection patterns need to work across all three workspace areas since different team members prefer different libraries. Also include a `WORKSPACE_GUIDE.md` that documents the folder conventions, naming standards for summary tables destined for Superset, and instructions for how new analysts should initialize their environment when they join the project.

We just finished refactoring the `<DataGrid />` component in our React + TypeScript monorepo at `~/repos/atlas-ui/packages/components/src/DataGrid/` — it was a single 1,800-line file and we've split it into `DataGridHeader.tsx`, `DataGridBody.tsx`, `DataGridPagination.tsx`, and a custom `useDataGridState` hook. Everything passes tests locally, but I want to make sure we handle the git side cleanly. Can you create a feature branch off `develop` called `feature/datagrid-refactor`, stage each new file in its own commit with conventional commit messages (e.g., `refactor(datagrid): extract header into DataGridHeader component`), make sure the deleted monolith file is tracked properly, and then open a PR against `develop` with a summary that lists the breaking changes (we renamed two exported props: `onSort` → `onSortChange` and `pageSize` → `defaultPageSize`) and includes a migration guide for consuming apps in the monorepo?

Our team maintains a Clojure microservices platform at `~/repos/billing-engine/` and we're about to refactor the invoice reconciliation module. Before I start, I need you to pull the full documentation tree from our Confluence page "Billing Engine – Reconciliation Logic" (space key `BILL`, page ID 918274) — read through it and all its child pages down to at least 3 levels so you understand the business rules, edge cases, and the state machine described there. Then, using what you learn from those docs, help me rewrite the `src/billing_engine/reconciliation/core.clj` namespace. The current implementation is riddled with mutable atoms tracking intermediate reconciliation state and uses nested `doseq` loops with side effects everywhere. I want an idiomatic functional approach — pure functions composing over immutable data, proper use of `reduce` and transducers for the line-item matching pipeline, and a clean separation between the reconciliation logic and the side-effecting persistence layer. Also, the docs mention a new "partial match with tolerance threshold" rule that was added last quarter on a child page under "Match Strategies" — make sure that gets incorporated as a new multimethod dispatch in the matching pipeline. Walk me through the design decisions as you go.

The tech lead assigned me a ticket to build out the game discovery and curation page for our indie game storefront at `~/repos/pixel-bazaar`. We're pulling data from the itch.io API to populate game listings, jam schedules, and creator profiles. The existing `src/services/itchClient.ts` has partial fetch logic for trending games and active jams, but it's broken — the pagination cursor isn't advancing, jam entries are missing their submission deadlines, and creator donation/tip links aren't being resolved correctly. I need you to fix the itch.io API integration so pagination works for both game search and jam listing endpoints, ensure each jam entry includes its start/end dates and submission deadline, and properly extract creator payment/support URLs. Then wire it all up to the existing Next.js page at `src/app/discover/page.tsx` — the tech lead wants three sections: "Trending Games" (with cover art, price, rating, and tags), "Active & Upcoming Jams" (sorted by submission deadline), and "Featured Creators" (with their top 3 games and a support/donate button). There are also failing tests in `__tests__/itchIntegration.test.ts` that need to pass green before I can mark this ticket done. Please make sure the code is clean, error states are handled gracefully (rate limits, missing data, API downtime), and everything matches the component interfaces already defined in `src/types/itch.d.ts`.

We're building a recipe sharing platform called "ForkIt" from scratch using a Node.js/Express backend with a React frontend and PostgreSQL. I need you to lay out a full development plan — break it into phases (MVP first, then social features like comments/ratings, then a meal planning calendar), define the task breakdown and iteration milestones for each phase, and for every phase generate the initial project scaffolding code including folder structure, module organization, API route files, shared utility modules, and database migration stubs so the team can hit the ground running with everything following consistent naming conventions and clean separation of concerns from day one.

We're building a public equipment rental request form for our manufacturing company's customer portal on our ERPNext site, and before I spec it out I want to understand what pain points other Frappe users have hit. Can you pull the recent issues from the `frappe/frappe` GitHub repository, analyze them for bugs, feature requests, and contributor-friendly issues — especially anything related to Web Forms, field validation, or file attachments — and give me a prioritized summary? Then, based on what you find, generate a Frappe Web Form definition for an "Equipment Rental Request" form that collects customer name, company, rental dates, equipment type (from a predefined list), quantity, a file upload for insurance certificates, and a comments field, making sure to avoid or work around any active bugs you identified in the report.

Our team maintains "VaultMesh," a secrets management and service mesh orchestration platform (Go microservices, gRPC, Envoy sidecar proxies, HashiCorp Vault integration, Postgres) used by enterprise clients to rotate credentials and manage mTLS certificates across multi-cloud deployments. We just opened a PR (#287) that adds a new "ephemeral token broker" service — it issues short-lived JWT tokens to workloads at runtime by calling Vault's Transit secrets engine, caches them in Redis with a sliding expiration, and exposes a gRPC streaming endpoint that sidecars subscribe to for token refresh events. The diff is about 1,400 lines across 11 files touching `broker/`, `cache/`, `proto/`, and `deploy/helm/`. I need a few things done together: first, do a thorough multi-model peer review of the PR — I want structured feedback on code quality, error handling in the gRPC streaming path, and whether our Redis cache invalidation logic has race conditions. Second, run a full security and threat model assessment of this new broker service, since it's sitting on a critical path for credential issuance — I'm especially worried about token replay attacks, cache poisoning via Redis, the blast radius if the broker is compromised, and whether our mTLS between the broker and Vault is properly pinned. Third, before we merge, I want to make sure this PR follows our repo's governance rules — it should be atomic (single concern), have evidence linking back to the design doc and threat model, and conform to our approval gates. Flag anything that should be split into separate PRs or that's missing required sign-off artifacts.

We're launching a new internal developer platform called "DevForge" that lets teams provision GitHub-based project repos through a self-service portal. I need three things done together: (1) Write up a full PRD for the MVP — it should cover user personas (platform engineers, team leads, individual devs), core features like repo provisioning, team access management, CI/CD template selection, and an approval workflow, plus success metrics and a phased rollout plan. (2) For the backend authentication layer, we need to authenticate as our GitHub App (App ID 284719) to list installations and then generate installation tokens so the portal can create repos and configure branch protections on behalf of users — walk me through the JWT signing flow using our `.pem` private key, show me the code for generating the JWT with the correct claims and expiry, exchanging it for an installation access token, and handling token refresh. (3) Both of these outputs need to be synthesized into a single coherent architecture document that ties the product requirements to the technical auth implementation — mapping each PRD feature to the specific GitHub API endpoints and permission scopes the JWT-authenticated app will need, so our engineering team has one unified reference doc instead of disconnected specs.

Our marketing agency's website is built with Astro and we're upgrading from v5 to v6 — we've already hit errors around our blog's content collections and the old `Astro.glob` calls breaking. At the same time, we're building an n8n automation that triggers a deployment workflow whenever new blog posts are published: I need help picking the right n8n-mcp tools to search for a GitHub node, validate the webhook trigger configuration, and chain it to our Vercel deploy step. Finally, we have a suite of integration tests in our CI pipeline that verify the content collection data flows correctly from the CMS API through our Astro build into the final rendered pages — several of those tests are failing after the upgrade and I need help analyzing the test output to figure out which failures are caused by the v6 migration breaking changes versus actual regressions in our CMS integration layer.

Our threat intel team just got a batch of raw IOC data (IP addresses, domains, file hashes) from a dark web paste linked to a campaign targeting financial infrastructure — I need you to parse and enrich those indicators, cross-reference them against MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and produce a structured intelligence report with TLP:AMBER marking. Simultaneously, we have a Foundry dataset at `ri.foundry.main.dataset.a]8f2c91-threat-iocs` that contains our historical IOC repository — use `pltr` to run a SQL query joining the new indicators against that dataset to find any overlaps with previously observed campaigns, and push the enriched results back as a new dataset under the `/Threat-Intel/2025-Q3/` folder in our Foundry project space (RID `ri.compass.main.folder.9e1b44a2`). Also, before you kick any of this off, I had a Playwright test suite running against our threat intel dashboard earlier today that crashed mid-run — there are orphaned Chromium processes still holding ports 3000 and 3001, and the Vite dev server for the dashboard frontend is still lingering. Kill all of that, free those ports, and wipe the `test-data/sessions/` directory so we have a clean slate, then proceed with the analysis and Foundry work.

I want to scaffold a new blog post for fabiorehm.com about building a real-time campaign analytics dashboard with Laravel Livewire — the post should walk through creating a Livewire 3 component that displays live-updating UTM parameter breakdowns, conversion tracking metrics, and channel performance charts for marketing campaigns, all without writing custom JavaScript. Before we scaffold the post structure, help me also draft the actual Livewire component code (using wire:model, polling, and Volt single-file components) that I'll embed as code samples, plus generate a sample set of UTM-tagged URLs and a measurement framework I can reference as the "example campaign" throughout the tutorial.

We're building "MotionDocs," an open-source library that wraps Android's ComposeWebView to render rich animated web content inside Jetpack Compose apps. I need help with three intertwined tasks. First, our flagship demo — a CSS/JS animation of a character performing a squash-and-stretch jump that intentionally violates traditional timing curves by using logarithmic easing and frame-skipping to create a glitchy, stylized motion aesthetic — is rendering incorrectly on certain API levels. The animation should feel like it's breaking the 12 principles on purpose (overshoot without follow-through, asymmetric arcs, deliberate spacing pops), so I need you to review the keyframe logic and fix the rendering while preserving the intentional rule-breaking. Second, we want to validate this fix using the RED-GREEN-REFACTOR subagent testing approach: first run the animation render tests *without* the fix to confirm they fail (RED), then apply the corrected animation code and confirm the tests pass (GREEN), then refactor to close edge cases like rapid lifecycle changes and WebView recomposition during mid-animation frames. Write the full test suite using this methodology with Compose UI testing and screenshot comparison. Third, all of this needs to be documented on our MkDocs site — update the existing ComposeWebView API reference pages, add a new guide under `docs/advanced/stylized-animations.md` explaining the intentional animation principle violations and why they produce the desired effect, wire it into `mkdocs.yml` nav, and make sure `mkdocs build --strict` passes with no warnings. Give me the animation keyframe fixes, the full RED/GREEN/REFACTOR test progression, and the complete MkDocs documentation updates.

We're designing a firmware update system called "DevicePilot" for our IoT fleet of industrial sensors. The system has two parts: a C-based embedded agent running on each sensor that receives and executes firmware commands (flash, rollback, verify, schedule, abort), and a Go orchestration service that manages update campaigns across thousands of devices. For the C agent, I want a clean Command Pattern implementation where each firmware operation is encapsulated as a command struct with execute/undo function pointers, a command queue with undo history, and a dispatcher that can serialize/deserialize commands from the wire format. For the Go service, I need well-designed interfaces — think `CommandDispatcher`, `DeviceConnection`, `CampaignStrategy`, `UpdatePolicy` — that let us swap transport layers (MQTT vs CoAP), plug in different rollout strategies (canary, blue-green, percentage-based), and mock everything for testing. Before any code though, I need you to produce a structured requirements catalog for the whole system: functional requirements covering all command types and their lifecycle, non-functional requirements around latency/reliability/resource constraints on the embedded side, interface contracts between the C agent and Go service, error handling and recovery scenarios, and traceability matrix mapping each requirement to the component (C agent or Go service) that implements it. Then show me the C command pattern implementation and the Go interfaces with example compositions.

Hey, we just finished a big sprint on our "Leavn" habit-tracking app and I need a few things done together. First, I wrote a paragraph for our README's "Getting Started" section but I rushed it and I'm sure there are grammar issues, awkward phrasing, and maybe some spelling mistakes — can you review it and suggest corrections without rewriting it? Here's the text:
"To getting started with Leavn, first you will need to clone the repositry and run npm install in the root directorie. After that, copy the .env.example file to .env and fill in you're database credentials and API keys. The app require Node.js version 18 or higher and a running PostgreSQL instance, which you can setup using the docker-compose file we have provided. Once everything is configurated, run npm run dev to start the development server, then navigate to localhost:3000 in your browser to began using the app."

Second, I need to commit the changes we made during this sprint. We updated the habit streak logic in `src/services/streakCalculator.ts`, added a new notification preferences page at `src/pages/NotificationSettings.tsx`, and fixed a timezone bug in `src/utils/dateHelpers.ts`. Can you commit these with a clear, conventional commit message summarizing the sprint work?

Third, I'm trying to understand how our reminder scheduling system works — specifically how `scheduleReminder` interacts with the notification queue and whether there's any retry logic if a push notification fails to send. Can you look through the codebase and explain how that flow works? I remember we had something in the services folder but I can't recall the exact file names or how they connect.

Thanks!
